claims.text: The applicable composition is precisely equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can be retained as a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution without secondary phases.
This solid solution has uniform elemental distribution and only minor lattice-strain distortions.
The equimolar CoCrFeNiTi solid solution has notably low hardness and strength.
Its low hardness and strength are governed predominantly by easy dislocation glide.
The CoCrFeNiTi solid solution has relatively high stacking-fault energy.
Low lattice distortion produces low barriers to dislocation motion.
Relatively high stacking-fault energy impedes deformation twinning in this alloy.
Modest lattice distortion and high stacking-fault energy limit activation of TWIP and TRIP.
Mechanical loading will produce dislocation accumulation and motion with little twinning or phase transformation.
Limited dislocation interactions prevent substantial increases in yield strength and hardness.
The starting alloy will exhibit low initial yield strength.
The starting alloy will exhibit a low strain-hardening rate.
Interstitial additions produce larger lattice distortions than substitutional elements and strengthen their interactions with dislocations.
A carbon-modified alloy is expected to have a higher strain-hardening rate than simple CoCrFeNiTi.
A carbon-modified alloy is expected to have higher hardness and yield strength than simple CoCrFeNiTi.
Carbon addition can promote TWIP while retaining TRIP in a compositionally tuned HEA.
Precipitate formation would introduce additional barriers to dislocation motion and increase hardness, yield strength, and strain hardening relative to the starting alloy.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to room-temperature, quasi-static loading and does not cover extreme temperatures or high-strain-rate loading.

contradictions.description: The mechanism presents relatively high stacking-fault energy as suppressing twinning, whereas the proposed carbon-based comparison invokes TWIP and the cited carbon example reports increased stacking-fault energy together with activation of TWIP. The hypothesis does not reconcile this non-monotonic or composition-dependent relationship.

The main hypothesis attributes the behavior jointly to low lattice distortion and relatively high stacking-fault energy and describes glide as dominant, but the falsification rule reframes it as being governed solely by easy glide due to low lattice distortion. Thus the rule tests a stronger and narrower claim than the stated hypothesis.
